episodes.text: Rejected at her first audition for the Imperial Ballet School for being too young and physically frail/sickly-looking; accepted a year later at age ten after re-applying.

Mocked by fellow students at the Imperial Ballet School with the nicknames 'the broom' and 'la petite sauvage' for a body shape (arched feet, thin ankles, long limbs) that did not match the era's preferred ballet physique; rather than being deterred, pursued additional intensive study under a sequence of premier instructors including Cecchetti.
Stated directly, as her own articulated philosophy: 'No one can arrive from being talented alone. God gives talent, work transforms talent into genius.'

When she attempted virtuosic fouette turns imitating a rival dancer's technique, her own teacher Pavel Gerdt reacted with anger and explicitly told her to stop trying to imitate physically stronger dancers, that her fragility -- not raw power -- was her real asset; she accepted this and did not pursue that style of virtuosic technique further.

Maintained a longitudinal, self-initiated pattern of five to six hours of daily rehearsal during training years, supplemented by private lessons in St. Petersburg and Italy, and continued seeking refresher study from Cecchetti after her formal training ended and after extended tours, rather than treating graduation as the end of skill development.

When a specific choreographed variation (the fairy Candide in The Sleeping Beauty) did not suit her own physical limitations (weak ankles), she revised the choreography herself without prior authorization, a modification that reportedly startled the ballet's own choreographer Petipa.

Danced with a distinctly unorthodox technical style (bent knees, imperfect turnout, unconventional arm positions) relative to her institution's strict academic classicism throughout her rise through the ranks, rather than conforming fully to the prevailing house style, even as this diverged from what her own training environment prized.

Self-choreographed and performed her own original solo piece, The Dragonfly, in costume of her own design (gossamer gowns with attached wings), distinct from her work interpreting others' choreography.
Kept a pet swan and personally studied its real movements over time specifically to make her performance of her signature role, The Dying Swan, more authentic.

Cast as the lead in Fokine's new ballet The Firebird for the celebrated Ballets Russes, she rejected the role specifically because she could not reconcile herself to Stravinsky's avant-garde musical score -- forfeiting a career-defining opportunity in one of the era's most historically significant new works rather than compromise her own artistic taste.

Refused to return to the Ballets Russes for a second season, preferring traditional melodic nineteenth-century ballet music and remaining skeptical of the company's more experimental artistic direction.

In 1912, slapped her dance partner Mikhail Mordkin during a curtain call, reportedly because she believed he was receiving more audience applause than she was, despite the pair having recently shared a major professional triumph together (ten curtain calls at a 1910 London performance).
In 1911, when her manager (and later husband) Victor Dandre faced embezzlement charges, personally requested that her own performance earnings be used to post his 35,000-ruble bail.

That same 1911 financial crisis, combined with her own stated desire for greater artistic freedom, directly preceded her decision to leave the secure, prestigious Imperial Ballet in 1913 and found her own independent touring company -- a financially riskier but ultimately far more lucrative path, described by one historical source as 'a very enterprising and daring act.'

For the first decade of running her own touring company, personally appeared on stage twice daily (assisted by only one other ballerina), maintaining what multiple sources independently describe as legendary stamina and work ethic.

As company director, exhibited a volatile leadership pattern described across multiple independent sources as alternating tantrums, refusals to perform, and sudden dismissals of company members with lavish parties and unexpected generosity toward them.

Personally recruited and trained roughly half a dozen young English dancers herself each year at her own home, then promoted the strongest performers to supporting company roles -- a sustained, hands-on talent-development pipeline rather than only hiring pre-trained dancers.

Led her company on tours logging several hundred thousand miles over roughly two decades, deliberately performing in venues and towns with no prior history of Western theatrical dance, including gymnasiums, warehouses, and bullfighting arenas rather than confining herself to established theatrical circuits.

On her 1929 Australian tour, when the ship carrying her company of about 42 dancers was advised against disembarking at the planned first port (Darwin), the tour proceeded to alternate regional Queensland towns with no prior ballet exposure; over the following four months the company gave 120 performances, and Pavlova -- then aged 48 -- personally danced in every single one.

Learned dance forms entirely outside her own classical training tradition (Mexican, Japanese, East Indian) from local teachers during her travels and incorporated them into her repertoire, including a pointe-shoe adaptation of the Mexican Hat Dance that became popular enough that Mexico declared it a national dance in 1924.

On a 1922 visit to India, commissioned and staged an original ballet, 'Ajanta Frescoes,' inspired by the Ajanta cave paintings she had seen -- a production critics judged amateurish, a documented public creative failure venturing into unfamiliar cultural material.

On that same 1922 India trip, after being introduced by a musician to a young Indian art student who also danced (Uday Shankar), had him choreograph and perform alongside her in new works -- an encounter she and her collaborators later described as 'accidental' that is credited with launching his career and, through it, a major strand of the modern Indian classical dance revival.

Personally mentored aspiring dancer Leila Sokhey (later known as Madame Menaka), who went on to found her own dance school in Bombay, and separately arranged formal ballet instruction for Rukmini Devi Arundale after meeting her by chance aboard a ship in 1929.
Attempted to initiate correspondence with the writer Rabindranath Tagore about creating a ballet based on his poetry; the project never materialized.

Personally devised a practical solution to a recurring technical problem in her own pointe shoes (adding hard leather to the soles and flattening the box), an innovation that eventually influenced modern pointe-shoe construction more broadly -- while also being documented as vain enough about how the modification looked that she had it removed or retouched from published photographs of her feet.

Sustained, deliberate ambiguity for many years about whether she and Victor Dandre were actually married -- at one point publicly declaring 'a true female artist must be consumed in her art' (implying she had refused marriage), yet telling reporters in 1924 that they had in fact been married since 1914, with no marriage certificate ever located.

Believed strongly that film could preserve and teach dance technique for future generations rather than viewing it as beneath live performance, and personally conducted her own recording experiments across several countries (filming in Java, slow-motion recording in Australia, sound recording in Hampstead) specifically to document her own repertoire for posterity.

Documented by at least one source as showing 'no interest in anything but her next performance' and as being 'considered by many people to be unintelligent,' apparently lacking conversational depth outside the subject of dance -- a narrow, near-total personal absorption in her craft.

After World War One, personally funded and established a home at Saint-Cloud near Paris housing fifteen Russian orphan girls displaced by the war, paid for through her own performance earnings plus solicited donations.

During her final illness, continued with rehearsal preparations despite being unwell, and against her doctor's explicit objections about her mounting fever, insisted on traveling on to the Netherlands specifically to keep her scheduled performance commitments.
Facing a diagnosis that survival required an operation that would likely end her ability to ever dance again, refused the surgery, stating directly: 'If I can't dance, I'd rather be dead.'

Her documented last words, as her health failed, were a request that her Swan costume be prepared -- asking, at the moment of death, for the specific costume of the role that had defined her entire career.
